title: A guided tour of cuckoo hashing
note: Prose lives here so it can be edited without touching code. Each figure is a small view that reads a recorded trace, so no number in this text is invented.

steps.title: One key, one drawer
body: A hash table turns a key into a drawer number. You put the key in that drawer, and later you look in that same drawer to find it.
The problem is that two different keys can give the same number. That is a **collision**, and every hash table is a different answer to it.

Cuckoo hashing gives an unusual answer. Each key gets **k** possible drawers instead of one. If the drawer a key wants is taken, the key pushes the current occupant out. The occupant must then go to one of *its* other drawers.

steps.title: Give every key k homes
body: Here are four words and a table of {{m}} buckets. Three hash functions give each word three bucket numbers.
This table of numbers is the whole contract of the data structure. Every word that the table holds is in one of its own {{k}} buckets, or on the stash.
Look at **ant** and **dog**. Two of their three numbers agree, so those two words have fewer than three different homes. Nothing in the reference sees this or corrects it.

steps.title: Where the numbers come from
body: The numbers are not decoration. Each one is SHA-256 of a seed and the word, read as one 256-bit number, reduced to the range of the table.
The seed of hash function *j* is the decimal number *j*, written as text. For three hash functions the seeds are the one-character strings "0", "1" and "2".
The digest below is real. You can produce it yourself with any SHA-256 tool.

steps.title: Divide a 256-bit number
body: A machine divides at most 128 bits at a time, and the digest is 256 bits. The reference therefore does the reduction in three steps, in base 2 to the power 64.
Each step keeps the remainder and puts it above the next 64 bits of the number. The last remainder is the bucket.
The result is the same as one 256-bit division. The three steps are how, not what.

steps.title: A lucky landing
body: An insert is a loop with a budget. Each turn of the loop does three things: it draws one hash function, it computes one bucket, and it looks at that bucket.
If the bucket is free, the element stays there and the insert is complete.
Use the arrows below to move through the first insert of this run.

steps.title: The coin flip nobody expects
body: Most descriptions of cuckoo hashing say: look at your k buckets, take an empty one. **This code does not do that.**
It draws one hash function at random and looks at that one bucket. The draw happens on every attempt, and that includes the very first one.
So a fresh element with two empty homes can still land on the occupied one and start a chain. The draw below decided which.
A question worth stopping on. Given only the table and the word, which bucket will the code look at? You cannot know. You must see the draw.

steps.title: The cuckoo move
body: When the bucket is taken, the code swaps. The new element goes in, and the old one comes out and becomes the element that must find a home.
This is a swap, not a search. The code does not ask whether the occupant has somewhere better to go.
The element that is out of the table is drawn above the row. Watch it change hands.

steps.title: Chains, and going back
body: One insert can move several elements. Each move costs one unit of the same budget, so a successful landing after four evictions used five of the attempts.
The budget belongs to the insert, not to the element. There is no separate allowance for the elements that were pushed out.
Because the draw is random, a walk can also come back to a bucket it already visited and swap the same pair again. That costs budget and gains nothing.

also.label: See a walk that goes back and forth

steps.title: When the walk stops
body: When the budget is gone, the element in hand has no bucket. The reference puts it on a **stash**.
It does not make a new set of hash functions. It does not build the table again. Most textbook treatments do both, and this code does neither.
The stash is outside the k-bucket contract, so it is drawn outside the row of buckets. A reader who checks only the k buckets will not find anything that lives there.

steps.title: The only hard failure
body: By default the stash has no limit, so an insert always succeeds. A caller can set a limit, and then a full stash makes the insert fail.
That is the one error the table can return. The message below is the exact text from the source, carried in the trace rather than typed into this page.

steps.title: Finding keys in k looks
body: A reader computes all {{k}} bucket numbers for the key and reads those {{k}} buckets. One of them holds the key, or the key is not in the table.
The cost does not grow with the number of keys. That is the point of the structure.
The reference table has no lookup method of its own. The code that does this is the client of the private-lookup protocol that the module was written for.

steps.title: Same keys, another table
body: The generator is a Mersenne Twister with the standard default seed, 5489, and the table never re-seeds it. So one order of inserts always gives one table, on every machine and every run.
Change the order and everything changes. The two runs below hold the same four words with the same parameters.
This is worth remembering when a test passes. It passed for that order.

steps.title: The production recipe
body: In the protocol the module was written for, the numbers are fixed: three hash functions, buckets equal to 1.5 times the number of records, and a budget equal to the number of records. The stash has no limit.
The product 1.5 times *n* is assigned to an integer, so it truncates. Five records give seven buckets, not eight.
Those parameters are chosen so the stash stays empty. The layer above copies only the table into the database it serves, so a reader cannot get a key on the stash at all.

steps.title: Drive one yourself
body: Here is a run you have not seen. Before each step, say what will happen. The answer comes from the recorded trace, so the exercise marks itself.
You need three things, and you already have them: the table of candidate buckets, the drawn hash function, and the current contents of the table.
If you can do this, you can read the reference.
